body: Tape comes squeaking off the roll in a church hall on a Saturday afternoon, and the man pulling it is up on a chair with a microphone in one hand and a broom handle in the other, because the stand has been broken since Easter and there is no money for another. The kit in the corner has one cymbal and a snare with a tea towel over it. A boy of about twelve is behind it playing something that will not be on tomorrow’s service sheet, and the man on the chair is not telling him to stop; he is winding the tape round the handle in time with it without noticing. Somebody’s mother comes in with a stack of chairs and asks whether anybody has seen the kettle. The boy does not stop playing. Nobody asks him to.

There is a tidy story about Caribbean gospel in which that boy is doing something borrowed. In it the church arrives late and reluctantly, picks up a popular rhythm from outside, and puts it to work to reach young people. It is the story told about a great deal of music, and it has the direction of travel backwards.
The rhythm was in the hall first. The charts came afterwards and took the credit, and the church, never good at defending itself on questions of this kind, largely let them.

Take the word riddim literally, because the word carries the argument. It does not simply mean a beat. In the tradition it names a piece of ground many different songs stand on — one rhythm, one bassline, held in common, voiced over by whoever has something to say this year. That is not a hook somebody owns. It is a shared possession, and a shared possession has to be held somewhere. It needs a room people come back to weekly, with the same instruments and mostly the same hands on them, where something worked out one Sunday is still there the next to be taken further. In many communities there was exactly one such room, and it had a cross on it.

This band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 on air. One is given to Afro-Caribbean worship outright — not a specialist hour in somebody else’s schedule, but a whole station on a permanent number.

Making that a station rather than an hour costs something, because it commits the band to the claim in public and forever. The safer arrangement is a slot: two hours on a Sunday evening, framed as outreach, which can be quietly dropped. A permanent frequency cannot, and it says out loud what a slot lets you leave unsaid. The drum was not borrowed from the dancehall. Both of them got it from the same place, and the church got there first.

The borrowed story is popular because it flatters everybody at once, which is generally how a wrong story survives. It lets the industry own the origin, which is worth money. It lets a nervous elder treat the drum as a concession to the young rather than something his own mother clapped to, which is easier than reconsidering forty years of caution. And nobody in that hall wrote any of it down, so the record ended up belonging to whoever pressed it. That is not a conspiracy. It is what happens when one party has a filing system and the other has a broom handle.

So the station is built as the older stream rather than an outreach idea. Zariah Inspire’s catalogue runs reggae, dancehall, soca and Afrobeats straight into teaching hymnody and gospel-soul, same frequency, same rotation, no handover apologising for the change of gear. Arranged that way, the ear learns what a playlist cannot teach: that the bassline under the dancehall track and the one under the hymn are relatives, and hearing them together is not a clash but a family resemblance nobody had pointed out.
Which brings up the objection raised in every hall like it, usually by somebody who has earned the right to raise it.

The objection is that this music is too much for worship — too physical, too close to the street, too easy to enjoy for the wrong reasons. Be fair to it. It is rarely snobbery and rarely about volume. It is nearly always a specific memory: somebody watched a rhythm that started in a congregation go out into the world and come back attached to things that ruined a person they loved, and concluded that the safest response was to leave the drum outside. But look at what that achieves. It hands the thing over. It concedes the rhythm to the world, and from then on the church can only borrow it back, and asking is how something that was yours becomes a loan.
The music is not the bait. It is the inheritance.

It is a Sunday afternoon and a man of sixty is peeling green bananas at his daughter’s sink while she talks to somebody in the hallway. Her speaker is on in the corner and he has not been paying it attention. Then he stops peeling, knife still in his hand, because the bassline underneath whatever this is happens to be one he last heard on an upright piano and a bass drum in his mother’s congregation, when he was small enough to be sat on a chair at the side and told not to move. He says nothing. When his daughter comes back he asks who this is, she tells him, and he goes back to the bananas. Four days later he rings and asks for the name again, and she can tell he has been looking for it all week.
Nobody argued him into that kitchen and nobody was going to. He had a position on the drum, formed long ago, and it did not survive four bars of something he recognised in his hands before his head.

It would be easy to leave that as a story about a man coming back, so it is worth saying he may not. People stop peeling bananas, go home, and nothing else happens, and a station counting those moments as results is lying to itself. And there is a genuine cost in the claim this article makes. Some of what came out of those halls went into the world and returned unrecognisable, used since for things that congregation would want no part of. Owning the origin of something is not owning what happened to it since.

But that is an argument for playing it, not putting it down. A rhythm nobody in the church plays any more is one the church has no say in. The only way to stop a thing being taken somewhere you would not follow is to keep going where it goes — to keep the drum in the room it came out of, weekly, with the tea towel on the snare. That is no compromise with the world. It is maintenance of something the congregation owns outright, and the elder who is cautious about it is guarding a possession he has been talked into thinking is a loan.

So the direction of travel matters. This is not an evangelistic use of somebody else’s sound, and the station need not apologise for the drum or justify it to a nervous board. It also settles the question of whether the music is too worldly for worship, in one line: the people who developed it were worshipping at the time. They were in the hall with a broken microphone stand, and they were not reaching anybody. They were praising, and the world was listening at the window.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Music, which is most of the band — worship, hymns, gospel, country, rap, ambient and much besides. Teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened rather than sung. Family programming, safe in a room with children in it. And the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them, 40 across 29 languages. Every station holds one frequency permanently, so a number found once can be gone back to without looking.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 311.50 — Riddim and Rhyme. It is Zariah Inspire’s Afro-Caribbean catalogue, reggae and dancehall and soca and Afrobeats married to teaching hymnody and gospel-soul, holding its frequency permanently rather than being an hour somebody defends each year. The reason to send you here is that this station is the argument in audible form. You cannot be talked into believing the drum came from the church; you can only hear it, and only if the hymn and the riddim are set next to each other by somebody embarrassed about neither. Leave it on for a week in a kitchen and the family resemblance stops being a claim in an essay and becomes something you cannot afterwards un-notice.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people reach for — which is how the next station for this music gets built bigger.

So take this as an invitation and not an offer. Put HM 311.50 on while you cook on Sunday, loud enough to reach the hallway, and get on with the cooking. And if there is somebody in the kitchen who stopped coming a long time ago, do not explain any of this to them. Let them stand there with a knife in their hand for four bars, and let them be the one who asks you who it is.
